# How AI could make decentralized applications easier to use


By OpenTools Team


·


October 5, 2026


Spend enough time in the crypto industry and one pattern begins to stand out. A user can make it through the first wallet connection, approve an initial transaction and still never return to the decentralized application. The problem isn't always a lack of interest. Sometimes, it’s the first few minutes that demand too much technical knowledge from someone who is still trying to understand what the application is asking them to do.


This is not just the experience of a few individuals. Many new users abandon a dApp after their first interaction, often before completing any transaction. Even Ethereum’s own user‑experience roadmap on ethereum.org acknowledges that “it is still too complex to use Ethereum for most people.” AI could help address part of the problem without hiding the mechanics underneath. For instance, AI could explain what is happening at the exact moment a question arises, rather than asking users to understand wallet prompts or network changes.


The same problem can appear before a user even reaches the transaction stage. Cryptocurrency users often need to check basic information about an asset before deciding what to do with it, and that information can change from one moment to the next. Someone checking[cryptocurrency prices today](https://www.binance.com/en/price) , for example, may not want to move between several different dashboards just to understand where an asset currently sits in the market. Binance's Cryptocurrency Prices page brings together current cryptocurrency prices and trading‑volume information, giving users a single place to check that context before moving on to a more technical interaction.


After all, AI doesn’t necessarily need to replace these information sources to make dApps easier. A more useful role could be helping users interpret the information they are already seeing, then connecting that understanding to the action they are considering.


## **How can AI simplify a user's first interaction with a dApp?**


AI can simplify the first dApp interaction by reducing the amount of unfamiliar information users have to process. Instead of executing a swap in three separate screens, a user can just state an outcome and let an[AI agent](https://opentools.ai/resources/30-agents-every-ai-engineer-must-build) handle the sequencing.


In the old flow, someone wanting to move funds has to find the right protocol, check the current rate, set a slippage tolerance, approve the token, and manually confirm the swap. These are five separate decisions, any of which can go wrong. But in[an AI‑assisted flow](https://opentools.ai/news/transform-your-workflow-with-these-5-game-changing-ai-apps) , the same person can type something like "show me the available USDC yield options on this chain" and get an explanation of every step before approving the transaction.


And this idea isn’t far‑fetched. Ethereum’s Pectra upgrade, which went live on mainnet on May 7, 2025, added EIP‑7702. In its April 2025 announcement, the Ethereum Foundation said the change supports “transaction batching, where multiple operations execute atomically within a single transaction,” as well as gas sponsorship, which lets another party pay transaction fees. That gives an AI assistant a practical way to bundle steps such as a token approval and a swap into a single request that the user still reviews and signs.


## **Could AI make dApps easier without taking control away from users?**


Yes, but only if AI is designed as an assistance layer rather than an automatic decision‑maker. Since users may control their own assets and cryptographic credentials in dApps, an AI assistant that automatically approves transactions could reduce friction while still making it harder for users to understand what their wallets are actually doing.


A better design would keep approval with the user while allowing AI to prepare the information needed for that decision. Wallet design is moving the same way. According to ethereum.org, the main contract for the ERC‑4337 account abstraction standard was deployed in March 2023, letting smart contract wallets offer recovery if keys are lost or stolen and better fraud detection. Those safeguards belong to the user’s account, not to the assistant.


Binance Research's 2026 work suggests that the relationship between AI and crypto is already moving beyond simple chat‑based assistance. Its April report on the shift from co‑pilots to agents described crypto as an early execution layer for agentic AI, pointing to blockchain's programmable rails and constant availability. Its analysis of Binance Ai Pro also found that 45.7% of conversations in a single‑day dataset were system‑triggered rather than initiated by a user prompt.


For dApps, this means AI could eventually handle some of the repetitive steps between a user's intention and an on‑chain action, while leaving meaningful approvals with the user.


Analytics platform DappRadar has also noticed AI's growing influence on dApp activity. In[a study updated in 2026](https://dappradar.com/blog/ai-agents-become-a-top-web3-investment-with-1-39b-raised?) , DappRadar noted that AI‑related on‑chain activity had reached approximately 4.5 million daily unique active wallets, highlighting that AI has already become a way for users to interact with blockchain‑based applications.


## **FAQ**


### **Does AI make dApps completely beginner‑proof?**


No. It reduces the number of decisions a new user has to get right, but it doesn't remove the underlying risks of self‑custody or market volatility.


### **Do I need to understand blockchain terminology to use an AI‑assisted dApp?**


Not for the basic flow. The assistant is designed to translate a plain‑language goal into the technical steps a dApp requires, while explaining fees and network choices along the way.
